body:
A retrospective of the 23 agent sessions behind two spec changes:

- #268 (tracking issue #269, tickets #270–#273)
- #277 (tracking issue #281, tickets #282–#288)

The sessions cost about $64: $14 for #269 and $50 for #281. They ran the briefs of Linewright 8c2638f, before the deployment moved to c8060e9, and each worked in a clone of `main` as it was then.

The work came out well. Every pull request but #276 passed CI on its first push, and none needed changes in review. The cost was in how the work was done. Each finding is a sub-issue, most severe first:

1. #300 Keep Linewright's secrets out of agent sessions and their transcripts
2. #301 Give work two tickets need its own ticket when cutting a spec change
3. #302 Keep an update run to the update
4. #303 Fix the shared build cache, which breaks when the session that started it ends
5. #304 Make a hung test name itself, locally and in CI
6. #305 Give agents a code map so they read less of the largest files
7. #306 Close the gaps the code reviewers left
8. #307 Catch with checks the mechanical mistakes the reviewers keep finding

## Already on `main`

What the same runs show about two changes merged since:

- **1b79095 (review once):** it saves about 3.5 minutes where a second review round ran. But those second rounds caught real bugs three times, so it goes with #306. It also makes #302 worse.
- **20276fe (the spec change's diff, and less of the spec read):** it changes little. Reading the spec cost 17–78K characters a run, against far more code.

## Seen along the way

These are about Linewright's own behaviour, not the agents' environment:

- Five tickets got an `implement-2` run that started and was cancelled 2–6s after the ticket closed.
- Each pull request gets two "Ready for review" comments.
- #292 and #291 merged before #290, whose ticket blocked #284 and #285. That forced two more update runs on #290.
title: Retro: the agents' environment, from the runs on #269 and #281
